summary: Discovery focused on unit economics: per-token pricing, batching/caching levers, and tradeoffs between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. Pendulum has a $100k quarterly inference budget target for initial pilot, strong latency SLOs (95th < 200ms for user-facing flows), and data residency constraints for some datasets. Redwood outlined hosted pricing tiers, reserved capacity discounts for Dedicated, and technical levers (batching, KV prefix cache, quantization) to reduce per-token cost. Agreed next steps: pricing spreadsheet, KV/cache doc, and a hands-on benchmark week-of 2026-12-20.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-10 20:00 UTC
Duration: 42 min
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Maya (Redwood CSM), Michael Chen (Pendulum Head of ML), Sara Lopez (Platform Eng), Rajiv Patel (CTO), Lina Gomez (Data Scientist)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, I'm Alex Martinez from Redwood, I'm joined by Priya our solutions engineer and Maya on CS. Can you all hear me okay?
[00:06] Michael: Yep, loud and clear, thanks Alex.
[00:08] Rajiv: Good, thanks.
[00:10] Alex: Great, quick agenda - want to understand your workloads, budget, SLOs and then walk through how different deployment modes impact unit economics, ok?
[00:18] Michael: That sounds good. For context, we are evaluating hosted first for speed but we're worried about per-token costs - we have a lot of inference volume for document summarization and some chat flows. Our tentative pilot budget is around $100k per quarter for inference to start.
[00:31] Priya: Thanks for the number - helpful. Do you have rough QPS and average prompt + response lengths?
[00:36] Sara: Typical peak QPS ~ 15 sustained, bursts to 60 QPS for 10-15 minutes. Average prompt ~ 120 tokens, average generation ~ 180 tokens.
[00:47] Priya: OK so ballpark token rate. Let me ask: what's the 95th percentile latency SLO for user-facing requests?
[00:52] Michael: We'd like 95th under 200ms if possible, but we'll accept up to 300ms during bursts. Batch processing (non-interactive) can be slower.
[00:59] Priya: Good - that matters a lot because batching helps unit cost but increases tail latency. For hosted, we can route low-latency flows to smaller batch sizes and background jobs to larger batching to save cost.
[01:10] Rajiv: Can you clarify the hosted pricing model? We saw your docs but unclear about per-token vs per-instance costs.
[01:16] Alex: Sure - hosted is per-token pricing with tiers. For example (ballpark) our standard gen price is $0.003 per 1k prompt tokens + $0.006 per 1k generated tokens on the hosted plan for open-model variants - actual depends on model size. Dedicated is a capacity commitment model - you reserve a pool (eg n GPUs) and you get a large discount on per-token compute and free intra-pool bandwidth; effectively your per-token is lower but you commit to spend. Private has a licensing/ops fee plus infra cost.
[01:41] Lina: So with Dedicated do we still get per-token metering?
[01:44] Priya: Yes you get metering and per-token attribution, but the invoice is dominated by the capacity commit. The economics are: if your steady-state throughput is high enough, Dedicated becomes cheaper per unit after you amortize the reserved capacity. We can model that for your QPS.
[01:58] Michael: Right, that's what we need - a model that shows break-even at different usage levels.
[02:02] Priya: We'll run a break-even analysis using your traces - it factors in batch sizes, KV cache hit rates, and quantization options. For example, enabling int8 quantization can reduce GPU memory and allow you to run more instances per GPU which lowers cost per token, but may introduce small quality diffs which you have to validate.
[02:19] Sara: How does KV/prefix caching work with short-lived sessions? Our chat flows often re-use prefixes but sometimes users do fresh context.
[02:26] Priya: We have a few caching levers. Prefix/KV caching stores key-value cache for repeated prefixes so repeated tokens or overlapping contexts don't re-compute attention. For chat, if the same user history or template is reused, you can get 40-70% token compute savings depending on reuse patterns. There's also request-level batching, and you can do hybrid routing: low-latency paths skip big batches and high reuse windows go to cached fast paths.
[02:45] Michael: That 40-70% sounds high - is that typical?
[02:49] Priya: It's workload dependent; if you have heavy template reuse it's on the higher end. We'll analyze your traces; even 20-30% is common and meaningful for cost.
[02:57] Rajiv: On the hosted plan, is there auto-scaling? Do you throttle?
[03:02] Alex: Hosted auto-scales within tenant quotas; we provide burst capacity subject to fair use, and you can set rate limits. For strict SLOs you may want Dedicated where you control a reserved pool and guaranteed throughput.
[03:13] Lina: If we did Dedicated, what's the timeline to provision?
[03:16] Alex: Typical Dedicated setup is 2-6 weeks depending on region and compliance needs; Private with on-prem is longer. For pilots we often start hosted while provisioning Dedicated.
[03:25] Michael: Ok good. On cost modeling - can you include real examples with batching? Like if we batch to 8 vs 32 what is per-token difference?
[03:33] Priya: Yes - rough example: with batch=8 you might see 1.0x baseline cost, batch=32 could cut per-token compute by ~25-35% on GPU due to kernel utilization, depends on model and sequence length. But bigger batches can add 50-150ms to P99 tails. For interactive SLOs you'll want adaptive batching - small batches for interactive, big batches for background.
[03:54] Sara: What about cache eviction and memory pressure? If we have many unique users are we losing cache benefit?
[03:59] Priya: Correct - cache hit rate correlates to user overlap. For many unique users you get less benefit. We also expose policies to pin high-value prefixes and TTLs; plus you can tier caching between node-local and a distributed cache.
[04:12] Michael: Security question - we handle sensitive portfolio data. Do you support KMS and audit logs?
[04:17] Alex: Yes - Hosted supports customer-managed keys via KMS for encryption at rest for higher tiers, and we provide audit logs and SSO/SAML for enterprise. Dedicated and Private give you more control. We'll attach SOC2/ISO summary.
[04:29] Rajiv: Any hidden costs around eg data egress or storage of KV cache?
[04:33] Priya: KV cache storage is included in the inference compute pricing for hosted, but long-term vector stores or embeddings persistence have separate charges. Data egress follows cloud provider rates; for Dedicated intra-pool traffic is cheaper. We'll show line items in the spreadsheet.
[04:47] Michael: For our $100k quarterly target - is that realistic for a pilot with our token volumes?
[04:52] Priya: Based on your rough volumes (15 sustained, bursts to 60, avg total tokens per request ~300) - let's do a quick calc: 15 QPS * 300 tokens * 3600 sec * 8 hours/day * 60 days is rough - ok that's messy live, we'll produce accurate numbers from your traces. But quick intuition: hosted could fit a small pilot within $100k if you optimize batching/caching and pick a mid-sized model; Dedicated likely needs higher steady state to justify commitments.
[05:18] Sara: One more - model variants: do you support smaller quantized variants for lower cost?
[05:22] Priya: Yes - we onboard quantized model variants and maintain compatibility. You can have routing rules to pick cheaper variants for lower-sensitivity calls and a higher-quality model for critical flows. That gives quality-cost levers.
[05:33] Michael: How do you measure unit economics per feature? We want to attribute cost to feature/team.
[05:38] Maya: In Console we provide per-route and per-model token breakdowns, token-level cost, and attribution tags so you can split by product feature or team. That helps show ownership of budget.
[05:48] Rajiv: What about SLA credits if latency spikes?
[05:51] Alex: SLA credits exist for Dedicated/Enterprise tiers, hosted has best-effort SLOs; Dedicated has formal SLA with remedies. We'll include SLA language in the enterprise packet.
[06:00] Lina: Can you show an example invoice?
[06:02] Alex: Yes we'll include a sample invoice showing per-token lines, reserved capacity amortization, and bandwidth/storage line items.
[06:08] Michael: Ok - sounds good, let's talk about the benchmark. We want latency and cost numbers with our actual traces.
[06:13] Priya: For the benchmark we'll need a week of sample traces and any blacklisted PII to mask. We'll run hosted and Dedicated simulations and show per-token cost at various batch sizes and cache hit rates.
[06:24] Michael: I'll send traces and SLO doc by Tuesday 12/15.
[06:28] Priya: Great - for the sim we'll run three scenarios: conservative cache (10% hit), typical (30%), optimistic (60%) to show sensitivity.
[06:36] Sara: Can you also show the impact of quantization on throughput?
[06:39] Priya: Yes, we'll include int8 vs fp16 throughput charts and a quality delta note.
[06:45] Rajiv: One procurement note - we have to align budget owners and procurement early; could you loop in your procurement contact on the next call?
[06:52] Maya: Absolutely - I'll invite procurement for the 12/20 follow-up.
[06:56] Alex: Recap: Redwood will send hosted vs dedicated pricing with examples, KV/cache whitepaper, SOC2 summary, and schedule benchmark week of 12/20. Pendulum sends traces and SLOs by 12/15.
[07:08] Michael: Yep, thanks everyone.
[07:11] Alex: Thanks, we'll follow up in email with attachments. Bye.

Notes: transcription has occasional mis-hears ("KV" appeared as "K-V" in a few spots), speaker labels are approximate.
